The boil-off rates need to remain low. Boil-off gas produced during flight operation can be routed directly to the propulsion system, whether for direct combustion in a gas turbine or fuel cell if any, thereby converting what might otherwise be a loss into useful energy. If boil-off gas exceeds propulsion demand, auxiliary storage tanks or venting systems would be required. The use of venting systems on aircraft could have an environmental impact as LNG predominately contains methane that has high global warming potential. Alternatively, advanced reliquefaction solutions can be installed to remove excess vapor without venting. 4.2.3 Liquified Ethane Deployment-Delivery, Storage, Dispensing, On-Site Liquification For commercial use of LE in aviation, pipeline networks would likely serve as the primary means of inland transport, even though LE itself cannot be moved through standard pipelines. For LE transport through pipelines, it is necessary ethane is in the gaseous phase. Regional gas transmission systems would carry ethane gas streams or already-separated ethane from upstream processing sites to purpose-built liquefaction facilities situated at major ports, central distribution hubs, or possibly airports. At airports they would require liquefaction on-site for efficient storage to meet the required demand. For domestic distribution after regasification, pipelines transporting gaseous ethane offer the most economical and operationally reliable option. In turn, marine carriers link these onshore pipeline grids, which could create a continuous and secure supply chain for ethane-based aviation fuel. Cryogenic road tankers have become a very effective way of delivering ethane to various industrial destinations beyond the fixed pipeline networks and marine transport. These include petrochemical plants, remote production sites, and possibly to airports in the future. The tankers are equipped with double-walled, vacuum-insulated tanks that can maintain the low temperature for ethane to remain liquid. Each unit usually holds from 30 up to 50 cubic meters, thus offering flexible delivery to sites without direct pipeline connections and those relying on periodic resupply. With the development in small-scale and micro-liquefaction installations, truck-based transportation options have grown in importance to serve operations. Besides highway transport, LE could also be moved by rail using cryogenic tank wagons or ISO- rated low-temperature tank containers. Rail transport would be the preferred option when pipelines do not exist, are uneconomical, or are infeasible; additionally, rail transport may provide access in areas where tankers cannot deliver the volumes required. Compared to marine transport, carrying ethane by train offers much larger shipment capacities and is far more efficient, though the high flammability and cryogenic properties of LE demand rigorous safety procedures. ISO-compliant cryogenic tank containers further facilitate intermodal transport, with the same unit able to transition between trucks, rail systems, and container vessels without the need for dedicated ships to carry ethane. Because they share a standardized form factor and have robust insulation, these containers can provide a flexible and scalable supply path to aviation fuel depots.
